extracted.intended_audience: logicians, philosophers, students of logic/language, and scientific writers
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and practical requirements for constructing and using a language fitted for philosophical and scientific inquiry, with emphasis on meaning, terminology, and descriptive precision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge of a word's history before redefining it
rubrics_metrics.description: Whoever seeks to introduce a more correct use of a term with important associations should possess an accurate acquaintance with the history of the particular word and of the opinions which in different stages of its progress it served to express.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To be qualified to define the name, we must know all that has ever been known of the properties of the class of objects denoted by it. If a new meaning would render false any proposition formerly held true under the old meaning, the proponent must be sure they have considered all that prior usage implied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not let any part of a word's meaning drop
rubrics_metrics.description: It may be good to alter the meaning of a word, but it is bad to let any part of the meaning drop.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When changing usage, avoid inadvertently losing portions of connotation that have functional importance; otherwise earlier true assertions may be invalidated or communication impaired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer the history of a word to dictionary glosses for real connotation
rubrics_metrics.description: The history of a word, by showing the causes which determine its use, is in many cases a better guide to its employment than any definition; definitions can only show its meaning at the particular time, or at most the series of its successive meanings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dictionaries give a blunt, broad meaning and often miss subtle collateral associations; study customary use, social/occasional associations, and historical development to understand real signification.

rubrics_metrics.name: When definitions are necessary, define according to current usage and preserve former senses
rubrics_metrics.description: The logician, not being able to prevent transformations, should submit to them when irrevocably effected, and if a definition is necessary, define the word according to its new meaning; retaining the former as a second signification, if it is needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept established changes in popular use; when fixing meanings for philosophical purposes, make the present sense explicit and record older senses as secondary to avoid confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: There should be no important meaning without its word
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever we have occasion to think of often, and for scientific purposes, ought to have a name appropriated to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A philosophical language must supply names for every important concept so that what is thought of frequently can be referred to unambiguously and efficiently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Descriptive Terminology: names to record individual observations exactly
rubrics_metrics.description: There ought to be all such names as are needful for making such a record of individual observations that the words of the record shall exactly show what fact it is which has been observed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Descriptive terminology must allow precise recording of observed instances (e.g., detailed botanical terms), enabling observers to state facts unambiguously and to compare instances for induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical/descriptive terms must be associated immediately with the perception they denote
rubrics_metrics.description: In order to derive due advantage from technical terms they must be associated immediately with the perception to which they belong; the term must be understood as directly as the most familiar word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fix technical terms by convention and, where possible, by direct sensory exemplification (e.g., color standards like 'apple-green' taught by showing), so the term summons the perception without conjecture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elementary sensations cannot be defined verbally; they must be taught by experience
rubrics_metrics.description: The names of elementary sensations, or elementary feelings of any sort, can not be defined; nor is there any mode of making their signification known but by making the learner experience the sensation, or by referring him to a remembered sensation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize limits of verbal definition: train perception or provide exemplars for terms that refer to raw sensations; definitions only suffice for compound or describable properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give distinctive names to frequent combinations to promote brevity and clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Brevity of description, and clearness, are greatly promoted by giving distinctive names not to the elements alone, but also to all combinations which are of frequent recurrence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create and fix compound terms for commonly occurring combinations (e.g., botanical compound terms, morphological classes) to allow concise, exact descriptions (examples: papilionaceous, pinnatifid, siliqua).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use standardized scales and numerical measures where practicable
rubrics_metrics.description: Some properties, as specific gravity, give at once a numerical measure; others require numerical scales (e.g., Mohs hardness) or classified scales (e.g., Werner's color scale) to convey precision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where possible, introduce agreed-upon numerical or graduated scales (hardness, color, size ratios) to fix distinctions that words alone would render vague.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of the twin processes: generalization and specialization of meanings
rubrics_metrics.description: Language undergoes two counter-movements: Generalization (words lose portions of their connotation and grow more general) and Specialization (words take on fresh connotation by being restricted to particular occasions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing or standardizing language, track how casual associations become part of meaning (examples: pagan, villain, loyalty) and how a genus-term can become a species-term; account for both tendencies when fixing terminology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard technical vocabulary against vulgarism and misuse
rubrics_metrics.description: Vulgarisms and ignorant or careless usage gradually deprive language of valuable modes of expressing thought (examples: 'transpire' used for 'happen', 'aggravating' for 'provoking', misuse of 'alone'), narrowing resources for precise expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor popular and translational corruptions (e.g., predicate/predict, demand/demander, transaction/compromis) and defend or rehabilitate technical distinctions when they are essential for clarity in science and philosophy.

rubrics_metrics.name: When preparing terms for induction, introduce an additional class of general names
rubrics_metrics.description: When we proceed from descriptive record to Induction, or to the comparison of observed instances preparatory to induction, we stand in need of an additional and a different sort of general names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond descriptive terms for individual observations, develop general abstract names suited for grouping and comparing instances in inductive reasoning (the text begins this point and implies the need to design such general terminology).

rubrics_metrics.name: Logicians can clarify meaning by stating the law of employment of a term
rubrics_metrics.description: Logicians cannot make the meaning of common words, but they can ascertain clearly what it is which, working obscurely, has guided the general mind to a particular employment of a name; and when they have found this, they can clothe it in such distinct and permanent terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a term's use is felt but not explicit, describe the underlying associations and social causes that have fixed its employment, then formalize that law of usage in precise, permanent terms to prevent future misapprehension.
